title: CELPIP General Listening — Practice Test 19
instructions: Listen to the audio for each part and answer the questions. Each audio plays once.

parts.title: Problem Solving
parts.description: A conversation in which one person has a problem and seeks help from another.

parts.title: Daily Life Conversation
parts.description: An everyday conversation between two people.

parts.title: Listening for Information
parts.description: An informational talk; listen for specific details.

parts.title: Discussion
parts.description: A discussion among people with different viewpoints.

parts.title: Viewpoints
parts.description: A longer talk presenting one speaker's opinion and reasons.

listeningScripts.title: An Estimated Gas Bill
listeningScripts.text: Caller: My gas bill is four hundred and ten dollars for the quarter. It is normally about a hundred and thirty. Agent: Let me look at the account. Was a meter reading submitted for this period? Caller: I don't think so. Agent: No, there wasn't. So the bill is an estimate, and the estimate is built from the same quarter last year plus the price change. Caller: I wasn't living here last year. I moved in in August. Agent: Then the estimate is built on somebody else's usage, and that is exactly the situation where these go wrong. Do you have a reading you can give me now? Caller: Yes. Zero-four-seven-nine-two. Agent: Thank you. That is considerably lower than the estimate assumed. I'll rebill the quarter on that reading, and the corrected figure comes to about a hundred and fifty. Caller: I've already paid the four hundred and ten. It went out by direct debit last week. Agent: Then the difference comes back to you, and you have a choice. It can go back to your bank in about ten working days, or it can sit as a credit on the account and reduce the next three bills. Neither is better than the other in money terms. Caller: I'd take the money back. Agent: Understood. One more thing, and this is the useful part. Submit a reading in the last week of every quarter and this cannot happen again. An estimate is only used when there is nothing else. The account accepts a reading up to five days before the bill date, and your bill date is the eighth. Caller: So the third is the last day. Agent: The third is the last day. Anything after that goes on the next quarter instead.

listeningScripts.title: A Book Club That Has Stopped Working
listeningScripts.text: A: We need to talk about the book club, because I nearly didn't come tonight. B: Three of us. Out of nine. A: Out of nine on the list. It hasn't been nine in the room since February. B: What has actually gone wrong? People liked it. A: Two things, and I think only one of them is fixable. The books have got long. Six hundred pages in four weeks, and most of us read on the bus. B: That's Fiona choosing. She reads two a week. A: She does, and she picks accordingly, and nobody wants to say so. B: What's the other thing? A: We moved it to Thursdays. Half the group has children's swimming on Thursdays, and they didn't say anything either. They just stopped coming. B: That one is easy. We move it back to Tuesday. A: Then let's do the easy one first and see who comes back. If it's the night, we'll know within a month. B: And the books? A: Cap it. Nothing over three hundred and fifty pages, and we rotate who chooses, so that it isn't a conversation about Fiona. B: I'll send the message. Not in the group chat — individually. People say what they actually think when it isn't in front of everybody.

listeningScripts.title: Bike Share Membership Briefing
listeningScripts.text: Welcome. Six things, and then you can go and use the thing. Your membership covers rides of up to forty-five minutes. After forty-five you are charged two dollars for each additional fifteen minutes, and that is the number people misremember. It is not a charge for going over the hour. It starts at forty-five. The way to avoid it on a long journey is to dock the bike at any station along the way and take it straight out again. Thirty seconds in the dock resets the clock. It does not have to be a different bike. Docking. A bike is not returned until the light on the dock turns green. An amber light means it has not latched and the ride is still running, and the commonest complaint we get is from somebody billed for four hours because they walked away on amber. If the station you want is full, use the app to claim a fifteen-minute grace extension. That is free, and it gives you time to reach the next station without the clock counting against you. Faults. If a bike is unrideable, don't just leave it in the rack for the next person. Report it in the app, and turn the seat backwards. The seat is the signal our crews look for, and it reaches them faster than the report does. And helmets are not provided. I would rather say that plainly now than have you looking for a box that isn't there.

listeningScripts.title: Manitoba Drug Coverage Portal
listeningScripts.text: Manitoba has opened an online portal that lets residents check whether a prescription drug is covered by the provincial plan before they reach the pharmacy counter. The plan covers about four thousand medications. Anything else is available only through an exceptional drug request made by the prescriber. The province says roughly one prescription in nine written in Manitoba is for something outside the standard list, and that most patients discover this at the till. The portal shows the coverage status, any quantity limit, and whether a cheaper listed alternative exists in the same class. It does not show what a patient will actually pay, because that depends on the deductible and on household income, and the province said building that in would have delayed the launch by a year. Pharmacists' organisations welcomed the portal but said the exceptional drug process itself remains the bottleneck, with a median wait of eleven days, and that a portal which tells people sooner that they face an eleven-day wait is an improvement of a limited kind. The province said a review of that process begins in the autumn.

listeningScripts.title: Cameras in the Parking Garage
listeningScripts.text: Fiorentino: Eleven break-ins in the garage since January, and two of those were the same car twice. Baptiste: I know. It was my car. And I still don't want cameras. Fiorentino: Which surprises people, so say why. Baptiste: Because a camera doesn't stop the eleventh break-in. It records it. And it also records me coming home at two in the morning, every night, for the next fifteen years. Shah: Both of those are true, and the second is the one boards underestimate. But the recording isn't the deterrent. The sign is. About sixty per cent of the effect of a camera system comes from people knowing that it is there. Baptiste: Then put up the sign and don't buy the cameras. Shah: That works for about four months. Word gets round when nothing is ever produced after an incident. Fiorentino: What if we keep the footage only for a short period? Shah: That is the sensible middle. Seventy-two hours, overwritten automatically, released only on a police request with a file number. You get the incident, and you don't get a fifteen-year record of anybody's movements. Baptiste: And who can look at it during those seventy-two hours? Shah: That is the question that actually matters, and the answer has to be nobody on the board. It goes to a managed service. If a resident can ask the chair to check who came in last night, you have built something else entirely. Fiorentino: I would want that in the bylaw, not in a policy that the next board can change. Shah: In the bylaw. And put the retention period on the sign, because that is a deterrent too.

listeningScripts.title: Compulsory Voting
listeningScripts.text: About two dozen countries require their citizens to vote, and a handful of those actually enforce it. The argument for it is usually made badly and the argument against it is usually made worse, so it is worth setting out what is actually known. The strongest claim for compulsory voting is not that it produces better decisions. It is that it removes a specific distortion. Turnout in a voluntary system is not random. It rises with age, with income and with education, and the gap is large — twenty to thirty points between the top and bottom income groups is typical. Politicians respond to the people who vote, which means that voluntary turnout quietly reweights the electorate towards the comfortable. Compulsion removes that reweighting, and the evidence from Australia is that it does so reliably. The objection I take seriously is not the liberty one, which usually dissolves on inspection: the fine is small, the ballot can be spoiled, and nobody is compelled to choose anyone. The serious objection is competence. If you compel attendance you bring in people who have not followed the campaign, and there is decent evidence that those additional voters are more susceptible to ballot order and to whichever name they happen to recognise. That is a real cost, and I do not think it is answered by saying that everyone deserves a say. So where does it land? On the evidence, the distortion removed is larger than the noise added. But I would put more weight than most people do on something else: this is a change to the rules of the game, proposed by people who are currently playing it. A reform that is right on the merits can still be corrosive if one side legislates it against the other. Do it with cross-party agreement, or do not do it at all.

questions.prompt: Why is the caller telephoning?
options: A quarterly bill is far higher than usual
A direct debit was taken twice
A meter has been read incorrectly by a visitor
A bill has arrived for the previous occupant
questions.correctAnswer: A quarterly bill is far higher than usual
questions.explanation: The bill is four hundred and ten dollars against a usual figure of about a hundred and thirty.

questions.prompt: Why was the bill an estimate?
options: The meter is inside a locked cupboard
The account was opened part-way through the quarter
No meter reading had been submitted
The reading submitted was rejected
questions.correctAnswer: No meter reading had been submitted
questions.explanation: No reading was submitted for the period, so the bill was estimated from the same quarter last year plus the price change.

questions.prompt: Why is this estimate particularly unreliable?
options: Prices changed twice during the quarter
It is built on the previous occupant's usage
The estimate covers four months rather than three
The meter was replaced in August
questions.correctAnswer: It is built on the previous occupant's usage
questions.explanation: The caller moved in only in August, so the previous year's usage belongs to somebody else — which the agent calls exactly the situation where estimates go wrong.

questions.prompt: What will the corrected bill come to?
options: About a hundred and thirty dollars
About two hundred and sixty dollars
About four hundred and ten dollars
About a hundred and fifty dollars
questions.correctAnswer: About a hundred and fifty dollars
questions.explanation: Rebilled on the reading given, the quarter comes to about a hundred and fifty — against the estimate of four hundred and ten already paid.

questions.prompt: What choice does the agent offer?
options: A refund to the bank, or a credit against the next three bills
A refund now, or a larger refund in three months
A credit on the account, or a reduced direct debit
A refund, or a reading taken by an engineer
questions.correctAnswer: A refund to the bank, or a credit against the next three bills
questions.explanation: The overpayment can go back to the bank in about ten working days, or sit as a credit reducing the next three bills.

questions.prompt: How does the agent compare the two options?
options: The credit is worth slightly more over time
Neither is worth more than the other
The refund costs a small administration fee
The credit is faster to arrange
questions.correctAnswer: Neither is worth more than the other
questions.explanation: The agent is explicit that neither option is better than the other in money terms, leaving it to the caller's preference.

questions.prompt: How can the caller prevent this happening again?
options: By changing the payment date on the direct debit
By asking for quarterly engineer visits
By moving to monthly billing
By submitting a reading in the last week of each quarter
questions.correctAnswer: By submitting a reading in the last week of each quarter
questions.explanation: An estimate is only used when there is nothing else, so a reading in the last week of each quarter prevents the situation entirely.

questions.prompt: What is the last day on which a reading will count?
options: The eighth of the month
The fifth of the month
The third of the month
The last day of the quarter
questions.correctAnswer: The third of the month
questions.explanation: The account takes a reading up to five days before the bill date, and the bill date is the eighth — so the third is the last day, and anything later counts towards the next quarter.

questions.prompt: How many people came this evening?
options: Nine, as usual
Three, out of nine on the list
Half of the group
Three, out of five who replied
questions.correctAnswer: Three, out of nine on the list
questions.explanation: B counts three in the room against nine on the list, and A notes it has not been nine since February.

questions.prompt: What does A give as the first problem?
options: The group meets too often
Nobody finishes the books at all
The meetings run late
The chosen books have become too long
questions.correctAnswer: The chosen books have become too long
questions.explanation: A names the length first: six hundred pages in four weeks, when most of the group reads on the bus.

questions.prompt: Why has nobody raised that?
options: It would mean saying something about Fiona's choices
The group has no way to vote on books
Fiona organises the meetings
Everybody assumed it was temporary
questions.correctAnswer: It would mean saying something about Fiona's choices
questions.explanation: Fiona reads two books a week and picks accordingly, and nobody wants to say so — which is why A proposes rotating the choice rather than naming her.

questions.prompt: What is the second problem?
options: The venue changed at the same time
Tuesday meetings were always better attended
Thursday clashes with children's swimming
Several members moved away
questions.correctAnswer: Thursday clashes with children's swimming
questions.explanation: The group moved to Thursdays, and half of it has children's swimming then; those members said nothing and simply stopped coming.

questions.prompt: Why will B message people individually?
options: The group chat has too many members
Not everybody uses the group chat
It is quicker than waiting for replies
People say what they think when it is not in front of everybody
questions.correctAnswer: People say what they think when it is not in front of everybody
questions.explanation: B deliberately avoids the group chat, on the grounds that people are franker one to one — which is the same reason the two problems went unsaid for months.

questions.prompt: When do additional charges begin?
options: After thirty minutes
After one hour
After forty-five minutes
After fifteen minutes
questions.correctAnswer: After forty-five minutes
questions.explanation: Membership covers rides up to forty-five minutes, and the speaker stresses that the charge starts there rather than at the hour, which is what people misremember.

questions.prompt: How can a longer journey avoid those charges?
options: By docking the bike briefly along the way
By booking the extra time in advance
By using two different bikes
By claiming a grace extension at the start
questions.correctAnswer: By docking the bike briefly along the way
questions.explanation: Docking at any station for thirty seconds resets the clock, and it does not have to be a different bike afterwards.

questions.prompt: What does an amber light on the dock mean?
options: The dock is full
The bike has been reported as faulty
The membership has expired
The bike has not latched and the ride is still running
questions.correctAnswer: The bike has not latched and the ride is still running
questions.explanation: A ride ends only on a green light; amber means the bike has not latched and the clock is still going.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker say is the commonest complaint?
options: Stations being full at peak times
Being charged for hours after walking away from an amber light
Bikes left unrideable in the racks
The forty-five minute limit being too short
questions.correctAnswer: Being charged for hours after walking away from an amber light
questions.explanation: The commonest complaint comes from people billed for four hours because they walked away while the dock was still showing amber.

questions.prompt: What should a rider do if the station is full?
options: Leave the bike beside the rack
Return to the previous station
Claim a free fifteen-minute grace extension in the app
Report the station in the app as faulty
questions.correctAnswer: Claim a free fifteen-minute grace extension in the app
questions.explanation: The grace extension is free and buys time to reach the next station without the clock counting against the rider.

questions.prompt: How should a faulty bike be signalled to the crews?
options: By leaving it outside the rack
By turning the seat backwards
By locking it to the end of the rack
By marking it in the app only
questions.correctAnswer: By turning the seat backwards
questions.explanation: The report goes in the app, but the seat turned backwards is the signal crews look for, and it reaches them faster than the report.

questions.prompt: What does the portal allow residents to do?
options: Order prescriptions online for collection
Apply for an exceptional drug request themselves
Compare prices between pharmacies
Check whether a drug is covered before reaching the pharmacy
questions.correctAnswer: Check whether a drug is covered before reaching the pharmacy
questions.explanation: The portal lets residents check coverage before the pharmacy counter, which is where the province says most patients currently find out.

questions.prompt: How many prescriptions fall outside the standard list?
options: About one in four
About one in nine
About four thousand a year
About one in eleven
questions.correctAnswer: About one in nine
questions.explanation: The province puts it at roughly one prescription in nine written in Manitoba.

questions.prompt: What does the portal not show?
options: What the patient will actually pay
Whether a cheaper alternative exists
Any limit on the quantity supplied
Whether the drug is covered at all
questions.correctAnswer: What the patient will actually pay
questions.explanation: Coverage status, quantity limits and cheaper alternatives are shown; the actual cost is not.

questions.prompt: Why is that figure missing?
options: Pharmacies set their own dispensing fees
The province does not hold that information
It depends on the deductible and household income, and would have delayed the launch
It changes too often to display
questions.correctAnswer: It depends on the deductible and household income, and would have delayed the launch
questions.explanation: The cost depends on deductible and household income, and the province said building it in would have put the launch back by a year.

questions.prompt: What did pharmacists' organisations say?
options: The portal will reduce queues at the counter
The exceptional drug process remains the real bottleneck
The four thousand listed drugs are too few
Prescribers will stop making requests
questions.correctAnswer: The exceptional drug process remains the real bottleneck
questions.explanation: They welcomed the portal but pointed to a median eleven-day wait on exceptional drug requests, calling a portal that reports that wait sooner an improvement of a limited kind.

questions.prompt: What is the scale of the problem?
options: Two break-ins since January
Eleven break-ins in fifteen years
Eleven break-ins since January
Sixty break-ins since January
questions.correctAnswer: Eleven break-ins since January
questions.explanation: Fiorentino opens with eleven break-ins since January, two of them the same car twice.

questions.prompt: Why does Baptiste object, despite being a victim?
options: A camera records a break-in rather than preventing it
Cameras would raise the service charge
The garage is too dark for cameras to work
He believes the break-ins have stopped
questions.correctAnswer: A camera records a break-in rather than preventing it
questions.explanation: Baptiste's own car was broken into twice, and his objection is that a camera does not stop the eleventh break-in — it records it, and records him for fifteen years besides.

questions.prompt: What does Shah say about deterrence?
options: Cameras deter only opportunistic thieves
Deterrence lasts about four months in any system
Recording quality matters more than placement
Most of the effect comes from people knowing the cameras are there
questions.correctAnswer: Most of the effect comes from people knowing the cameras are there
questions.explanation: Shah puts about sixty per cent of the effect of a camera system down to people knowing it exists — the sign rather than the recording.

questions.prompt: Why is a sign alone not enough?
options: Signs are removed or defaced
Word spreads once nothing is ever produced after an incident
Insurers require actual recording
A sign cannot state a retention period
questions.correctAnswer: Word spreads once nothing is ever produced after an incident
questions.explanation: Shah says a sign without cameras works for about four months, until word gets round that nothing is ever produced after an incident.

questions.prompt: What middle course does Shah propose?
options: Recording only between midnight and six
Cameras at the entrance but not inside
Keeping footage for seventy-two hours and overwriting it automatically
Keeping footage until an incident is closed
questions.correctAnswer: Keeping footage for seventy-two hours and overwriting it automatically
questions.explanation: Seventy-two hours, overwritten automatically, released only on a police request with a file number: enough for the incident, not enough for a record of anybody's movements.

questions.prompt: Who should be able to view the footage?
options: The chair, on a resident's request
Any resident whose car was affected
The board, by majority decision
A managed service, and nobody on the board
questions.correctAnswer: A managed service, and nobody on the board
questions.explanation: Shah calls this the question that actually matters and answers it directly: a managed service, and nobody on the board.

questions.prompt: Why does that matter so much?
options: Otherwise a resident could ask the chair to check on somebody
The managed service is cheaper than staff time
Police will only accept footage from a third party
Board members change every year
questions.correctAnswer: Otherwise a resident could ask the chair to check on somebody
questions.explanation: Shah's reasoning is that if a resident can ask the chair to check who came in last night, the building has built something other than a security system.

questions.prompt: What does Fiorentino insist on?
options: That the cameras be reviewed after a year
That the arrangement go into the bylaw
That residents vote on the retention period
That the sign not mention the cameras
questions.correctAnswer: That the arrangement go into the bylaw
questions.explanation: Fiorentino wants it in the bylaw rather than in a policy the next board could change, and Shah agrees, adding that the retention period should go on the sign.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker call the strongest claim for compulsory voting?
options: That it produces better decisions
That it removes a distortion in who turns out
That it reduces the cost of campaigning
That it is popular where it has been tried
questions.correctAnswer: That it removes a distortion in who turns out
questions.explanation: The speaker sets aside better decisions and rests the case on removing a specific distortion in the composition of the electorate.

questions.prompt: What pattern does voluntary turnout follow?
options: It varies mainly between regions
It falls steadily at every election
It depends on how close the contest is
It rises with age, income and education
questions.correctAnswer: It rises with age, income and education
questions.explanation: Turnout is not random: it rises with age, income and education, with a typical gap of twenty to thirty points between the top and bottom income groups.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker say that matters?
options: Low turnout makes results unpredictable
Older voters are more likely to change their minds
Politicians respond to the people who actually vote
Campaigns cost more where turnout is uneven
questions.correctAnswer: Politicians respond to the people who actually vote
questions.explanation: Because politicians respond to those who vote, voluntary turnout quietly reweights the electorate towards the comfortable — which is the distortion compulsion removes.

questions.prompt: Which objection does the speaker dismiss?
options: That compulsory voting infringes liberty
That it would be expensive to enforce
That turnout would not actually rise
That no large country has ever tried it
questions.correctAnswer: That compulsory voting infringes liberty
questions.explanation: The liberty objection dissolves on inspection for the speaker: the fine is small, the ballot can be spoiled, and nobody is compelled to choose anyone.

questions.prompt: Which objection does the speaker take seriously?
options: That spoiled ballots would become too numerous
That compelled voters are more swayed by ballot order and familiar names
That fines fall hardest on the poorest
That governments would stop campaigning
questions.correctAnswer: That compelled voters are more swayed by ballot order and familiar names
questions.explanation: The serious objection is competence: compelling attendance brings in people who have not followed the campaign, and the evidence is that they are more susceptible to ballot order and recognised names.

questions.prompt: What condition does the speaker attach?
options: That it be introduced with cross-party agreement
That the fine be set high enough to work
That it be trialled in one region first
That spoiled ballots be counted separately
questions.correctAnswer: That it be introduced with cross-party agreement
questions.explanation: The speaker weighs the rules of the game being changed by people currently playing it, and concludes that it should be done with cross-party agreement or not at all.
